paragraphs: The first of these errands was at Madame Hohlakov’s house. He hurried over, wanting to get it done quickly so as not to be late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been a little unwell for three weeks. For some reason her foot had swollen, and although she was not in bed, she lay all day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir, in a fascinating but decorous _déshabillé_. Alyosha had noticed once, with innocent amusement, that despite her illness she had begun to take a good deal of trouble over her dress. Top-knots, ribbons and loose wrappers had appeared. He had an inkling why, though he pushed the thought away as frivolous. For the past two months the young official Perhotin had been calling at the house regularly.

Alyosha had not been there for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight up to Lise, because she was the one he needed to talk to. Lise had sent a maid to him the day before with a special request that he come and see her “about something very important,” and for certain reasons that request interested Alyosha. But while the maid was gone to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived and at once sent a message begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was best to give in to the mamma’s request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise’s room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on her couch. She was dressed with particular elegance and was obviously in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

“It’s ages, ages, absolutely ages since I’ve seen you! A whole week—just think of it! Oh, but of course you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You’ve come for Lise. I’m sure you meant to creep up to her room on tiptoe so I wouldn’t hear you. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But we’ll come to that later, though it’s the most important thing, later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust my Lise to you completely. Since Father Zossima died—God rest his soul!” (she crossed herself)—“I’ve thought of you as a monk, even though you look so charming in your new suit. Wherever did you find a tailor like that in this town? No, no, that’s not the main thing—later. Forgive me for calling you Alyosha now and then; an old woman like me can take liberties,” she smiled coquettishly; “but that can wait as well. The important thing is that I don’t forget what’s important. Do remind me yourself. The minute my tongue runs away with me, you just say, ‘the important thing?’ Ach! How can I know now what matters most? Ever since Lise took back her promise—that childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, to marry you—you’ve understood, of course, that it was only the playful whim of a sick child who’d been shut up in her chair for so long—thank God she can walk now!... And that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow, for your unhappy brother, who tomorrow will—But why talk about tomorrow? The mere thought of tomorrow makes me ready to die. To die of curiosity.... That doctor was here yesterday and examined Lise.... I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that’s not the point, that’s not the point again. You see how I’m mixing everything up. I’m in such a rush. Why am I in a rush? I can’t make it out. It’s dreadful, the way I seem to be losing the power to understand anything. It all feels like one big tangle. I’m afraid you’re so bored that you’ll leap up and run off, and that will be the last I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here without coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”
Alyosha hastened to thank her. He had only just had coffee, he said.
“Where?”
“At Agrafena Alexandrovna’s.”

“At ... at that woman’s? Oh, she’s the one who’s brought ruin on everybody. Not that I know anything about it. They say she’s turned into a saint, though it’s rather late in the day. She should have done it earlier. What good is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I have so much to tell you that I’m afraid I’ll end up telling you nothing. This awful trial ... I’m certainly going, I’m making arrangements. They’ll carry me there in my chair, and anyway I can sit up. I’ll have people with me. And, you know, I’m a witness. How am I to speak, how am I to speak? I don’t know what I’ll say. You have to swear an oath, don’t you?”
“Yes, but I don’t think you’ll be able to go.”

“I can sit up. Oh, you’ve muddled me! Oh, this trial, this savage deed, and then they’re all off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all of it so fast, so fast, everything changing, and in the end—nothing. Everybody grows old with death ahead of them. Well, so be it! I’m weary. Katya, that _cette charmante personne_, has let down all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her and settle in the nearest town, and they’ll all torment one another. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all is the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Oh, and would you believe it, one of them says I was ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s ——, I can’t bring myself to say the horrid word. Just fancy, just fancy!”
“Impossible! Where did it appear? What did it say?”

“I’ll show you in a moment. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here, in the Petersburg paper _Gossip_. It only started this year. I’m terribly fond of gossip, so I take it, and now it’s paying me back—so this is what gossip comes to! Here, this passage. Read it.”
And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that she had kept under her pillow.

She was not exactly upset so much as overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really was in a tangle in her head. The item was typical of its kind and must have been a great shock to her. But perhaps it was lucky that she could not hold her mind on any one subject just then. In a minute she might race off to something else and forget the newspaper altogether.

Alyosha knew very well that the story of the terrible case had spread over the whole of Russia. And, good heavens, what wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs and about himself he had read during those two months, along with other equally credible news! One paper had gone so far as to say that he had entered a monastery and become a monk, out of horror at his brother’s crime. Another denied this and said that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken open the monastery chest and “made tracks from the monastery.” The piece in _Gossip_ carried the headline “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk.” (That, alas, was the name of our little town. Until now I had kept it secret.) It was short, and Madame Hohlakov was not named in it. In fact, no names appeared at all. It said merely that the criminal, whose coming trial was causing such a sensation—a retired army captain, an idle swaggerer and reactionary bully—was forever entangled in love affairs, and was a special favorite with certain ladies “who were pining in solitude.” One of these ladies, a pining widow who tried to look young although she had a grown-up daughter, was so infatuated with him that only two hours before the crime she had offered him three thousand roubles, if he would run away with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had preferred to murder his father and take the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia with the middle-aged charms of his pining lady. This playful piece closed, naturally, with an outburst of generous indignation at the wickedness of parricide and at the recently abolished institution of serfdom. Alyosha read it with curiosity, then folded the paper and gave it back to Madame Hohlakov.

“Well, that’s me, of course,” she hurried on. “There’s no doubt I’m the one they mean. Not much more than an hour before it, I’d suggested gold mines to him, and now they say ‘middle-aged charms,’ as if that were my reason! He wrote that out of spite! May God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, as I forgive him! You know it’s— Do you know who it is? It’s your friend Rakitin.”
“Perhaps,” said Alyosha, “though I’ve heard nothing about it.”
“It’s him, it’s him! Don’t say ‘perhaps.’ You know I threw him out of my house.... You know the whole story, don’t you?”
“I know you asked him not to visit you anymore, but I haven’t heard why ... from you, at any rate.”
“Ah, so it was from him you heard it! He runs me down, I suppose, runs me down dreadfully?”
“Yes, he does; but then he abuses everybody. And I haven’t heard from him why you dropped him, either. I hardly ever see him now, in fact. We’re not friends.”

“Well, then, I’ll tell you everything. It can’t be helped, I’ll make a confession, since there is one point where I may have been at fault. Only a tiny, tiny point, so tiny it hardly counts. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly turned arch, and a charming, enigmatic smile played on her lips—“you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you.... No, no, just the opposite. I’m speaking to you now as if you were my father—mother is quite out of place. Well, it’s as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that’s exactly it. I called you a monk just now. So then, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can’t be angry with him. I’m cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have got it into his head that he’s in love with me. I only noticed later. At first, a month ago, he merely began coming to see me more often, nearly every day, though of course we knew each other before. I suspected nothing ... and then all at once it dawned on me, and I started noticing things, with astonishment. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who’s in the service here, became a regular visitor. You’ve met him here ever so many times yourself. And he’s such an excellent, serious young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not daily (though I’d be glad to see him daily), and always so well dressed. In short, I love young people, Alyosha, talented and modest ones, like you. And he has nearly a statesman’s mind, he talks so charmingly, and I’ll certainly, certainly try to get him promoted. He’s a diplomat in the making. On that awful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin turns up in such boots, and always stretches them out on the carpet.... Then he began to hint at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell right after he’d pressed my hand like that. He’d met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he’s forever sneering at him, snarling at him, for no reason I can see. I simply watched the two of them together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone—no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone when suddenly in comes Rakitin, and just fancy! He’d brought me some verses of his own writing—a little poem about my bad foot, that is, he’d described my foot in a poem. Wait a moment—how did it go?
A captivating little foot.

It began something like that. I can never remember poetry. I have it here. I’ll show it to you later. But it’s a charming piece—charming; and, you know, it isn’t only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I’ve forgotten it; it was just right for an album, in fact. So of course I thanked him, and he was plainly flattered. I’d barely finished thanking him when in walks Pyotr Ilyitch, and Rakitin suddenly turned black as night. I could see Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, since Rakitin obviously wanted to say something after handing me the verses. I had a presentiment of it; but there was Pyotr Ilyitch. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses without saying who wrote them. But I’m convinced he guessed, though to this day he won’t admit it and swears he had no idea. He says that on purpose, though. Pyotr Ilyitch started laughing right away and began picking them apart. ‘Wretched doggerel,’ he called them, ‘some divinity student must have written them,’ and with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. ‘Good gracious!’ I thought, ‘they’ll go for each other.’ ‘I wrote them,’ he said. ‘I wrote them as a joke,’ he said, ‘because I think it’s degrading to write verses.... But they’re good poetry. They want to put up a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women’s feet, whereas I wrote mine with a moral purpose, and you,’ he said, ‘are a defender of serfdom. You have no humane ideas,’ he said. ‘You have no modern, enlightened feelings, progress hasn’t touched you, you’re a mere official,’ he said, ‘and you take bribes.’ Then I started screaming and pleading with them. And, you know, Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward. He immediately put on the most gentlemanly tone, gave him a sarcastic look, heard him out, and apologized. ‘I had no idea,’ he said. ‘I wouldn’t have said it if I’d known. I’d have praised them. Poets are all so touchy,’ he said. In short, he mocked him under cover of that most gentlemanly tone. He explained to me afterwards that it was all sarcasm. I thought he meant it. Only, as I lay there, just as I’m lying before you now, I wondered, ‘Would it be the proper thing for me to throw Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a visitor in my house, or would it not?’ And, would you believe it, I lay here with my eyes shut, wondering whether it would be proper or not. I worried and worried, my heart began to pound, and I couldn’t decide whether to raise an outcry or not. One voice seemed to tell me, ‘Speak,’ and the other, ‘No, don’t speak.’ And the moment the second voice had said that, I cried out, and fainted. Naturally, there was a commotion. I suddenly got up and said to Rakitin, ‘It pains me to say it, but I don’t wish to see you in my house again.’ So I threw him out. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I know very well I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn’t really angry with him at all; but I suddenly imagined—and that was what did it—what a fine scene it would make.... And yet, believe me, it came quite naturally, because I really did shed tears and cried for several days afterwards, and then one afternoon I suddenly forgot all about it. So it’s two weeks now since he’s been here, and I kept wondering whether he’d come back. I wondered even yesterday, and then last night this _Gossip_ arrived. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it off, and they printed it. That was two weeks ago, you see. But, Alyosha, it’s dreadful how I go on talking and never say what I want to say. Ah! The words just come by themselves!”
